title: Rappelling & Abseiling
summary: Getting down safely is a skill in its own right. A controlled rappel on snow, rock or ice is one of the most reliable ways out of a bad situation.
steps: Back up the rope, keeping both ends brakeable: never tie off a single strand you cannot hold.
Set up your anchor equalised and redundant, ideally masterpointed, and equalise before loading.
Back up the system with a second tie-in: a lock-off or a knot in the standing strand.
Descend facing downhill with weight on the brake strand; keep the device above your waist.
tip: Rappel on an ice axe: weight on the shaft-side strand, free-hanging on the spike, and step down the face as you go.

title: Crevasse Rescue
summary: If a partner falls into a crevasse you have minutes, not hours. Every rope team must be able to haul 100 kg out of a hole in ice.
steps: Immediately build an anchor: ice screws, a snow picket or a buried pack, and get the casualty talking.
Lock the rope to the anchor so the system can hold weight even if you are pulled forward.
Run a mechanical advantage haul: a Z-pulley, a 3:1 or the drop-loop method, one person hauling at a time.
Belay the hauling end hard; raise in short pulls with clear communication.
tip: Practise with an empty pack on a rope over a crevasse before you ever need it for real.

title: Avalanche Rescue
summary: Companion rescue is the single most important survival skill in the mountains. Most buried climbers are alive when they stop moving.
steps: Switch your transceiver to search, count and time; keep it on your body so the signal keeps broadcasting.
Sweep the avalanche debris in a systematic grid; probe in a 60 × 60 pattern with a strong, steady probe.
Once you feel a body shape, shovel from downhill to upward, digging a wide deep pit and leaving the face on the uphill side.
Clear the airway, check for avalanche debris in the airway, rewarm gently and treat for trauma.
tip: Everyone carries a transceiver, probe and shovel, and all three are practised together before any trip leaves base camp.

title: Weather Forecasting
summary: On the big peaks the weather decides everything. Reading it early is the difference between a summit day and a rescue.
steps: Check a mountain-specific forecast, not just the valley: the summit can be 15 °C colder and far windier.
Read pressure trends: a rapid drop means low cloud, falling temperatures and a rising chance of snow.
Spot clouds building over summits through the day: start early, be back in the valley by early afternoon.
Agree a turnaround time and forecast window before leaving, and tell someone your route and return time.
tip: Wind is the deciding factor on summits. Learn to read the mountain's own wind and pick the sheltered side of the ridge.

title: Snowcraft & Anchors
summary: On snow, ice and mixed ground there is no bolt for a hand, so you build your own: knots, pickets, screws and deadman systems.
steps: Tie solid, load-bearing anchors: hand grips, a chest hitch, a Munter, a clove or the lark's foot.
Carry three or four snow pickets as backup; test every anchor by pulling hard before you clip in.
Know how to place a deadman anchor in a snow pit and how to protect a vertical wall.
Clean snow anchors as you go, and re-test them after wind, thaw or a long rest.
tip: A wall of poured snow can hold several body weights — but not if the snow is wet, hollow or sliding.

title: Rope Work
summary: The rope is the climbing team's lifeline. Sound rope work means choosing the right system for the terrain, tying reliable knots, and communicating clearly.
steps: Tie in with a re-threaded figure-eight on a bight, finished with a stopper knot, and check your partner's knot every time.
On glaciers, rope up at 8–10 m intervals with butterfly knots or prusik-friendly spacing so a fall can be arrested by the team.
Coil the rope in the 'mountaineer's coil' for carrying; keep it dry and away from crampon points.
Agree and rehearse rope commands: 'On belay?', 'Belay on', 'Climbing', 'Climb on', 'Take', 'Slack'.
tip: A dry rope is a strong rope. Wet or icy ropes can lose a significant fraction of their dynamic strength, so protect them from meltwater.

title: Belaying
summary: Belaying is the act of managing the rope so that a falling climber is caught safely. It demands full attention from the first move to the last.
steps: Use a tube or assisted-braking device; always keep a brake hand on the rope and never let go.
Stand close to the wall and slightly offset so the fall line is clear; give a soft catch by stepping or jumping lightly.
Perform a partner check before every climb: harness, knot, device, locking carabiner, rope end.
On multi-pitch, build anchors that are redundant, equalised and strong enough to hold a factor-2 fall.
tip: Most belay accidents are human error. Pause, look at the system, and say it aloud.

title: Crampon & Ice Axe Use
summary: Crampons and ice axes turn frozen slopes into secure terrain. Efficient technique saves energy and keeps you safe on steep snow and ice.
steps: Flat-footing (French technique): keep all points biting on moderate slopes, ankles flexed.
Front-pointing: kick straight in with the front points on steep ice, heels low, hands about shoulder height.
Carry the axe in the uphill hand, spike in the snow, adze forward, and plunge it with every step on a traverse.
Always check that crampons fit your boot before a climb and that anti-balling plates are fitted.
tip: Walk with feet slightly wider than normal so crampon points never snag your trousers or boots.

title: Self-Arrest
summary: A fall on a steep snow slope can accelerate within seconds. Self-arrest is the single most important snow-travel skill and must be practised until instinctive.
steps: Grip the axe with one hand on the head (thumb under the adze) and the other on the shaft near the spike.
Roll towards the axe, pulling the pick into your shoulder at chest level and kicking your toes up, off the snow.
Dig the pick in with your chest weight over it and your hips low; spread your legs wide for stability.
Practise falling head-first, on your back and face-down so the response is automatic.
tip: Remove crampons or keep points clear: kicking a crampon into the slope while falling can flip you over or cause serious injury.

title: Route Finding
summary: Reading terrain is half of mountaineering. Good route finding avoids objective hazards and finds the most efficient line to the summit and back.
steps: Study the route beforehand: topos, satellite imagery, guidebooks and recent conditions reports.
Look for natural weaknesses: ribs and ridges are safer than gullies, which funnel rockfall and avalanches.
Set a turn-around time and stick to it, regardless of how close the summit appears.
Mark the route with GPS waypoints and, where appropriate, wands or cairns for the descent.
tip: Look back often. The descent looks completely different from the ascent, so memorise landmarks as you climb.

title: Acclimatization
summary: The body needs days or weeks to adapt to lower oxygen pressure. Slow, staged ascent is the most reliable protection against altitude illness.
steps: Above 3,000 m, increase your sleeping altitude by no more than 300–500 m per night, with a rest day every 3–4 days.
'Climb high, sleep low': make day trips to higher altitude, then descend to sleep.
Hydrate well, eat carbohydrate-rich food, and avoid alcohol and sedatives.
Descend immediately if symptoms of acute mountain sickness worsen or do not improve with rest.
tip: Fitness does not prevent altitude illness. The fittest climbers are often those who ascend too fast.

title: Navigation
summary: Whiteout, darkness and fog can make familiar terrain unrecognisable. Navigation combines map, compass and modern GPS tools, and a margin for error.
steps: Orient the map, take a bearing, and walk in short, verified legs. Count paces and note time in poor visibility.
Use a handrail (a ridge, stream or cliff edge) and a catching feature beyond the target to avoid overshooting.
Carry a GPS or phone with offline maps as a backup, never as the only tool.
Know how to calculate declination and set it on your compass for your region.
tip: Fresh batteries are a navigation tool. Keep electronics warm inside your jacket to preserve charge.
